title: Consensus in Effective Model Inference for Disordered Ising Systems
abstract: When independent learners are trained on data from the same disordered system, finite and noisy samples can lead them to different descriptions of the underlying physics. We quantify the reproducibility of such descriptions through consensus, the degree of agreement among independently trained models. In a teacher-student framework on the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model, an ensemble of students each infers a single uniform effective coupling from a finite set of equilibrium configurations drawn from one quenched bond realization. Aggregating the inferred couplings across students and realizations yields the consensus distribution, whose width quantifies the agreement among learners. The variance of this distribution separates exactly into a finite-sampling contribution, bounded below by inverse of Fisher information, and a quenched-disorder contribution. Sum of these two variance is minimized near critical region, so the consensus width has a minimum near the pseudocritical temperature that sharpens with increasing disorder. The two minima arise from different mechanisms: the sampling term inherits the critical peak of the Fisher information, while the disorder term is temperature-independent at leading order and acquires its critical minimum only at fourth order in the disorder strength, through the covariance between the linear and cubic responses to the bond disorder. Because the students fit a uniform coupling to a heterogeneous lattice, the inferred coupling also carries a misspecification bias that survives in the infinite-data limit. This bias displaces the minimum of the mean-squared error above the consensus minimum, so the temperature at which independent learners agree most closely is not the temperature at which their shared answer is most faithful.
summary: This work introduces 'consensus' to measure how robustly different models agree on the effective physics of disordered systems. By analyzing the variance of inferred parameters, the authors show that the best temperature for agreement is distinct from the best temperature for accuracy due to model limitations. This provides a crucial diagnostic tool for interpreting results from complex, disordered physical models.
main_problem: The paper quantifies the reproducibility of inferred physical descriptions (effective parameters) from finite, noisy data generated by disordered systems, using the concept of 'consensus'.
main_result: The temperature at which independent learners agree most closely (consensus minimum) is generally different from the temperature where their shared answer is most faithful (MSE minimum) due to inherent model misspecification bias.
method: A teacher-student framework is employed where multiple students independently infer a single effective coupling from finite subsets of equilibrium configurations generated by a disordered Ising system.
model_or_system: The system is the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model on a square lattice with quenched couplings drawn from a uniform distribution. The inference process involves fitting a single uniform effective coupling to the local field statistics.
key_observables: Consensus Width (variance), Mean-Squared Error (MSE), Sampling Noise variance, Quenched-Disorder variance, Residual Complexity (RC).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($\delta$), Temperature ($T$), Finite sample size ($M$), and the number of students ($N_s$).
main_assumptions: The students are restricted to fitting a single uniform effective coupling, which introduces a systematic misspecification bias that persists even in the infinite-data limit.
figures_summary: Figures compare the inferred coupling $ ar{J}$ across different kernels, showing consistency at certain temperatures, and illustrate Residual Complexity (RC), which is zero for the isotropic kernel but non-zero for the identity kernel, indicating lost structure.
paper_structure: The paper develops the consensus concept by decomposing the total variance into sampling and disorder contributions. It then analyzes the bias introduced by the limited hypothesis class, comparing the optimal temperature for consensus agreement versus optimal faithfulness (MSE).
why_interesting: The rigorous framework for quantifying model uncertainty and disagreement (consensus) in the presence of quenched disorder is highly relevant for interpreting complex simulations in condensed matter theory, especially when data is limited or noisy.
